items.where: Fixing ATP Signaling if Cortisol Isn't High, P2
items.your_version: Your ketone strategy decides how you handle salt, since the salts bring their own sodium while the diet drains it. If you're in a crisis and need the fog to lift fast, there's Strategy A, the "Crisis Mode". You drink BHB (beta-hydroxybutyrate) salts and keep eating a standard low-sugar diet. In trials, ketone esters, salts and MCT oil improved thinking a little against a placebo, from a single dose as well as over two weeks or more (Bonnechère, et al, 2026). Amazon reviews do show many folks noting increased mental clarity, though. And one study shows large improvement for Parkinson's, and [one woman's Alzheimer's was reversed] (https://www.longecity.org/forum/viewtopic.php?t=1025608). Data on ketones for PTSD specifically are sparse.

items.title: DMSO in the Glutamate Shield, with your 1967 paper
items.your_version:
DMSO (99.9%): Smell it, as in the Fog table below. In rat brain cells in a dish, DMSO at 0.5 to 1.5% quickly turned down the signals glutamate sends through its NMDA and AMPA receptors, and the calcium they let in. It also kept glutamate from killing the cells (Lu & Mattson, 2001). Back in 1967, doctors in Lima injected it into the muscles of 42 psychiatric inpatients, and nine of them had severe anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Within days they grew calmer, and the acute cases went home sooner than 16 patients with similar diagnoses who got the usual treatments of the time, such as electroshock, insulin comas and tranquilizers (Ramírez & Luza, 1967). There was no placebo, though, and the patients they were compared with weren't picked at random. 

It is used for humans routinely in stem cell transplants and by many humans, including children, for all kinds of medical problems, as it treats hundreds of them ([Jacob & De La Torre, 2015](https://www.amazon.com/Dimethyl-Sulfoxide-DMSO-Trauma-Disease/dp/1498714676)). No trial has tested it for PTSD, so for PTSD it rests on what people report, and many say it helps.

Nebulized DMSO has been shown to prevent toxic cotton smoke from killing 4/6 sheep in one study ([Brown, et al, 1988(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3356738/)]). It has shown some neurotoxic effects in other rodent studies under other conditions.

My experience and that of those I know and have read about, is that it has immense brain benefits, turning bad trips good instantly, giving relaxed alertness, more intelligence, brighter mood (especially when nebulized), but when used too close to bedtime or too much, it can reduce sleep. If it is killing my neurons, I'm pretty sure it's killing the trash ones that should be going out anyway. My dad used DMSO for decades and was healthy and mentally sharp into his old age.

items.my_version: DMSO (99.9%): Smell it, as in the Fog table below. In rat brain cells in a dish, DMSO at 0.5 to 1.5% quickly turned down the signals glutamate sends through its NMDA and AMPA receptors, and the calcium they let in. It also kept glutamate from killing the cells (Lu & Mattson, 2001). Back in 1967, doctors in Lima injected it into the muscles of 42 psychiatric inpatients, and nine of them had severe anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Within days they grew calmer, and the acute cases went home sooner than 16 patients with similar diagnoses who got the usual treatments of the time, such as electroshock, insulin comas and tranquilizers (Ramírez & Luza, 1967). There was no placebo, though, and the patients they were compared with weren't picked at random. In a second dish study, DMSO at 0.5% and 1% killed rat brain cells by itself, and injections of it set off widespread cell death in young mice's brains (Hanslick, et al, 2009). So if you're pregnant, don't use it, and keep it away from children. Nobody has measured how much reaches your brain when you smell it. And no trial has tested it for PTSD, so for PTSD it rests on what people report, and many say it helps.
